desc:
A histogram is given by the array heights: bar i has width 1 and height heights[i]. For a bar i, look at the longest block of consecutive bars that contains bar i and in which every bar is at least as tall as bar i. The number of bars in that block is the reach width of bar i.

Return an array widths where widths[i] is the reach width of bar i. (A bar's reach width times its height is the area of the widest rectangle that uses the full height of that bar.)

Example: for heights = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the answer is [1, 6, 2, 1, 4, 1]. Bar 4 (height 2) can stretch left over the bars of height 6 and 5 and right over the bar of height 3, but the bar of height 1 stops it: the block is bars 2 to 5, four bars.
hints: Expanding left and right from every bar until a shorter bar appears is correct but can take O(n<sup>2</sup>) time. What do you really need to know about each bar?
Only two things: the nearest bar to the left that is strictly shorter, and the nearest bar to the right that is strictly shorter. The reach width is the gap between them, minus one.

Find the nearest strictly shorter bar on one side with a stack of indices whose heights increase: pop every index whose height is not smaller than the current bar, and the index left on top (if any) is the answer. Repeat from the other side.
editorial: Let L[i] be the index of the nearest bar to the left of i that is strictly shorter than bar i (or -1), and R[i] the nearest strictly shorter bar to the right (or n). Every bar strictly between them is at least as tall as bar i, and the two bars at the ends are shorter, so the block is exactly L[i]+1 .. R[i]-1 and the reach width is R[i] - L[i] - 1.

Both boundaries are found with a monotonic stack. Scanning left to right, keep a stack of indices with strictly increasing heights. For the current bar, pop while the top has height ≥ the current height; those bars are not strictly shorter and can never be the nearest shorter bar for anything later that is not blocked by the current bar. The index now on top is L[i]; then push i. A mirrored right-to-left pass gives R[i]. Every index is pushed and popped at most once per pass, so the time is O(n) and the space O(n). This exact building block powers the largest-rectangle-in-histogram solution.
solution:
def barReachWidths(heights):
    n = len(heights)
    left = [-1] * n
    right = [n] * n
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]:
            stack.pop()
        right[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n
        stack.append(i)
    return [right[i] - left[i] - 1 for i in range(n)]
